# What changes at Sanctuary Sound?

At Acme, exact ages supplied offspring birth years. Here, dolphins are released
and their ages are treated as uncertain in the kin analysis. A sampled dolphin
can be the mother of a daughter born **after** its capture, provided it survives
until that birth. Neither member of a pair is assigned a parent/offspring role
from its measured length alone.

We follow Mark's `fit_delfi_S.r` through the age-length calibration and category
counts. Then we expand **one** category over its possible ages. We do not yet
fit the demographic model or implement the efficient full likelihood.

Preparation remains visible below. Repeated calculations are functions in
`R/tidy-delfi-S.R`, ordered as we use them. The core analysis needs the same
packages as the Acme notebook; Mark's packages are used only by the optional
cross-check at the end.

# Meet the data and supplied growth model

## Choose the data file

Change `data_path` for your copy of Mark's repository. As in the Acme notebook,
relative paths resolve from the Rmd's folder when knitting. `helper_path` points
to the companion functions in this CKMRshiny checkout.

```{r load-data}
data_path <- normalizePath(params$data_path, mustWork = TRUE)
loaded_data <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
loaded_names <- load(data_path, envir = loaded_data)
stopifnot("samp_delfi_S" %in% loaded_names)
raw_data <- loaded_data$samp_delfi_S
rm(loaded_data)

samples <- as_tibble(unclass(raw_data$Samps))
pairs <- tibble(pair_id = seq_len(nrow(raw_data$POPs)),
                id_1 = raw_data$POPs[, 1], id_2 = raw_data$POPs[, 2])
public <- attr(raw_data, "public")
Amat <- public$Amat

stopifnot(!anyNA(samples$ID), !anyDuplicated(samples$ID),
          all(pairs$id_1 %in% samples$ID), all(pairs$id_2 %in% samples$ID),
          all(pairs$id_1 != pairs$id_2))
# Assert each unordered individual pair occurs only once.
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(tibble(first = pmin(pairs$id_1, pairs$id_2),
                               second = pmax(pairs$id_1, pairs$id_2))))

samples |> slice_head(n = 6) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
tibble(sampled = nrow(samples), recorded_POPs = nrow(pairs),
       known_ages = sum(!is.na(samples$A)),
       nonlethal_samples = sum(!samples$LETHAL)) |> knitr::kable()
```

**The recorded ages are calibration data here.** Mark's comments describe a
small set of animals that failed to survive release. In the current dataset,
all 2,530 samples have ages and all are marked non-lethal. His calibration uses
all available ages, pooling sexes. The subsequent kin analysis ignores each
individual's recorded age. We will make that separation explicit.

The file records POPs in parent/offspring order. We will use that information
only to recognize that a pair is related; category counting below forgets the
orientation and the probability calculation allows either individual to be the
mother. `secret` simulation attributes are not used.

If `kinsimmer2` is absent, loading may warn that its namespace was replaced by
`.GlobalEnv`. That concerns stored simulator functions. We use the recorded
columns and extract four supplied constants; the tidy calculations do not call
those simulator functions.

## Make the growth parameters visible

The supplied `public$len_fun` is a **quantile** function for length given age.
Its enclosing environment stores the growth constants. We extract those values
once into an ordinary list, then pass them explicitly through the calculations.
They are supplied inputs: we are not estimating them from these samples.

```{r growth-parameters}
length_function_environment <- environment(public$len_fun)
growth <- mget(c("vb_Linf", "vb_k", "vb_t0", "vb_cv"),
               envir = length_function_environment, inherits = FALSE)
rm(length_function_environment)

tibble(parameter = names(growth), value = unlist(growth, use.names = FALSE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 6)
```

Mean length at age is

\[
\mu_a=L_\infty\{1-\exp[-k(a-t_0)]\}.
\]

Length given age has a gamma distribution, with shape $1/\mathrm{CV}^2$ and
scale $\mu_a\mathrm{CV}^2$. Thus its mean is $\mu_a$ and its CV is constant.
The known-age samples below show why a length is not an exact age measurement,
especially as growth approaches its asymptote.

```{r growth-and-recorded-ages}
samples <- samples |>
  mutate(epoch = factor(if_else(Y <= 2015, epoch_levels[1], epoch_levels[2]),
                        levels = epoch_levels))
age_grid <- 1:40                            # Mark's full calibration age support.
year_grid <- seq.int(min(samples$Y), max(samples$Y))
growth_curve <- tibble(age = seq(1, 40, length.out = 300)) |>
  mutate(mean_length = growth$vb_Linf * (1 - exp(-growth$vb_k * (age - growth$vb_t0))))

samples |>
  filter(!is.na(A)) |>
  ggplot(aes(A, LENGTH)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = epoch), alpha = 0.22, size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = growth_curve, aes(age, mean_length), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            color = "#263740", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = epoch_colors, limits = epoch_levels) +
  labs(x = "Recorded age (calibration only)", y = "Length", color = "Sampling epoch",
       caption = "Dark curve: supplied mean length at age. Points: known-age calibration samples of both sexes.")
```

# From continuous lengths to length bins

Mark chooses length boundaries from 1.50 to 2.00, spaced by 0.05. We retain
both open-ended tails: below 1.50 and at least 2.00. The lower boundary belongs
to the bin on its right. The dashed vertical lines mark these same boundaries
in every plot with length on the x-axis.

```{r define-length-bins}
Lbin_cuts <- seq(1.5, 2.0, by = 0.05)
length_bins <- delfi_s_length_bins(Lbin_cuts)
samples <- samples |>
  mutate(bin_id = findInterval(LENGTH, c(-Inf, Lbin_cuts, Inf))) |>
  left_join(select(length_bins, bin_id, length_bin), by = "bin_id",
            relationship = "many-to-one")
stopifnot(!anyNA(samples$bin_id), !anyNA(samples$length_bin))
length_bins |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)

samples |>
  ggplot(aes(LENGTH, fill = epoch)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.025, boundary = 1.5, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Lbin_cuts, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey35", linewidth = .35) +
  facet_wrap(~epoch, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = epoch_colors, limits = epoch_levels) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  labs(x = "Length", y = "Sample count",
       caption = "Dashed lines: calibration bin boundaries. Both sexes contribute to calibration.")
```

## Calculate probabilities in the bins

For bin $\ell=[l_\ell,u_\ell)$, integrate the conditional length density:

\[
g_{\ell a}=P(L_b=\ell\mid A=a)=F_a(u_\ell)-F_a(l_\ell).
\]

The tail endpoints are $-\infty$ and $+\infty$, giving CDF values zero and one.
This replaces the dummy tail values used in Mark's script with explicit bounds.

```{r length-given-age-probabilities}
length_probs <- expand_grid(age = age_grid, bin_id = length_bins$bin_id) |>
  left_join(length_bins, by = "bin_id", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  mutate(mean_length = growth$vb_Linf * (1 - exp(-growth$vb_k * (age - growth$vb_t0))),
         gamma_shape = 1 / growth$vb_cv^2,
         gamma_scale = mean_length / gamma_shape,
         lower_cdf = pgamma(lower, shape = gamma_shape, scale = gamma_scale),
         upper_cdf = pgamma(upper, shape = gamma_shape, scale = gamma_scale),
         p_length_given_age = upper_cdf - lower_cdf)

length_probability_checks <- length_probs |>
  summarise(total = sum(p_length_given_age), .by = age)
stopifnot(all(length_probs$p_length_given_age >= 0),
          max(abs(length_probability_checks$total - 1)) < 1e-12)

length_probs |>
  filter(age %in% c(2, 5, 15, 40)) |>
  select(age, length_bin, p_length_given_age) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = age, values_from = p_length_given_age, names_prefix = "age_") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

First look at continuous densities. Then compare the probability masses in the
bins. Their heights represent **probability per bin**, not a density; the tail
bins continue beyond the displayed length range.

```{r continuous-length-densities}
illustrated_ages <- c(2, 5, 15, 40)
length_limits <- range(c(samples$LENGTH, Lbin_cuts)) + c(-0.05, 0.05)
# Show almost all of the model densities, even beyond the selected sample's
# observed lengths. The binned plots below explicitly clip only their tails.
density_limits <- qgamma(c(0.001, 0.999), shape = 1 / growth$vb_cv^2,
                        scale = range(length_probs$mean_length) * growth$vb_cv^2)
length_densities <- expand_grid(age = illustrated_ages,
                               length = seq(density_limits[1], density_limits[2], length.out = 600)) |>
  mutate(mean_length = growth$vb_Linf * (1 - exp(-growth$vb_k * (age - growth$vb_t0))),
         density = dgamma(length, shape = 1 / growth$vb_cv^2,
                          scale = mean_length * growth$vb_cv^2))
length_densities |>
  ggplot(aes(length, density, color = factor(age))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Lbin_cuts, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey55", linewidth = .3) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = .85) +
  labs(x = "Length", y = "Density", color = "Age",
       caption = "These are P(length | age) densities, before using any age prior.")
```

```{r binned-length-probabilities, fig.height=5.5}
length_probs |>
  filter(age %in% illustrated_ages) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = pmax(lower, length_limits[1]), xmax = pmin(upper, length_limits[2]),
                ymin = 0, ymax = p_length_given_age, fill = factor(age)), color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Lbin_cuts, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey45", linewidth = .3) +
  facet_wrap(~age, ncol = 2, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = .85) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = length_limits) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  labs(x = "Length bin (outer bins extend beyond this view)", y = "Probability in bin")
```

The full table can also be viewed as a heat map. At a fixed age, probabilities
sum to one across length bins. At a fixed length bin, they generally do **not**
sum to one across ages: that requires Bayes' rule.

```{r forward-probability-heatmap, fig.height=5.5}
length_probs |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = pmax(lower, length_limits[1]), xmax = pmin(upper, length_limits[2]),
                ymin = age - .5, ymax = age + .5, fill = p_length_given_age)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Lbin_cuts, color = "white", linewidth = .25) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "P(bin | age)") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = length_limits) +
  labs(x = "Length bin", y = "Age",
       caption = "Each horizontal age slice sums to one across bins. Tail bins are clipped only for display.")
```

# Calibrate age given length, separately for two epochs

## An age prior and Bayes' rule

Let $d_e>0$ be the decline parameter for epoch $e$. Mark assumes

\[
\pi_e(a)=\frac{\exp(-d_e a)}{\sum_{u=1}^{40}\exp(-d_e u)},\qquad
P(A=a\mid L_b=\ell,e)=
\frac{g_{\ell a}\pi_e(a)}{\sum_u g_{\ell u}\pi_e(u)}.
\]

The helper `delfi_s_age_key()` implements those multiplications and normalizations
as joins and grouped operations. It takes `log_decline` so that $d_e$ is positive.

For a provisional $d=0.2$, inspect what goes into one bin's posterior:

```{r inspect-bayes-calculation}
provisional_key <- delfi_s_age_key(log(0.2), length_probs)
provisional_key |>
  filter(bin_id == 6, age <= 10) |>
  select(length_bin, age, p_length_given_age, p_age, joint_probability,
         p_length_bin, p_age_given_length) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 6)
```

`p_length_bin` is the same denominator on every row of this bin. Dividing the
joint probabilities by it makes the age probabilities sum to one.

## Count the known ages and fit the two declines

The calibration likelihood is conditional on the observed length bins. If
$n_{e,a,\ell}$ counts known-age samples, its parameter-dependent part is

\[
\ell_e(d_e)=\sum_{a,\ell}n_{e,a,\ell}
\log P(A=a\mid L_b=\ell,e).
\]

This is **not** a fit to the length histogram alone. The recorded ages identify
which age probabilities receive each observed count. As in Mark's script,
we use all known ages of both sexes before restricting the kin-analysis sample.

```{r count-aged-samples}
aged_counts <- samples |>
  filter(!is.na(A)) |>                          # Known ages are used only at this stage.
  count(epoch, age = A, bin_id, name = "n_aged") |>
  complete(epoch = epoch_levels, age = age_grid, bin_id = length_bins$bin_id,
           fill = list(n_aged = 0L))             # Explicit zeros over the calibration grid.

stopifnot(sum(aged_counts$n_aged) == sum(!is.na(samples$A)),
          all(samples$A[!is.na(samples$A)] %in% age_grid))
aged_counts |>
  summarise(known_age_samples = sum(n_aged), .by = epoch) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r fit-age-priors}
age_fits <- setNames(lapply(epoch_levels, function(e) {
  optimize(
    f = function(log_decline) delfi_s_calibration_loglik(
      log_decline, filter(aged_counts, epoch == e), length_probs),
    interval = log(c(0.01, 0.9)), maximum = TRUE
  )
}), epoch_levels)

calibration_fits <- tibble(
  epoch = factor(epoch_levels, levels = epoch_levels),
  log_decline = vapply(age_fits, function(f) f$maximum, numeric(1)),
  decline = exp(log_decline),
  conditional_log_likelihood = vapply(age_fits, function(f) f$objective, numeric(1))
)
calibration_fits |> knitr::kable(digits = 6)

# Recompute each key explicitly at the returned optimum; no environment state
# from an optimizer's last evaluation is needed.
age_key <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(calibration_fits)), function(i) {
  delfi_s_age_key(calibration_fits$log_decline[i], length_probs) |>
    mutate(epoch = calibration_fits$epoch[i], .before = 1)
}))
key_checks <- age_key |>
  summarise(total = sum(p_age_given_length), .by = c(epoch, bin_id))
stopifnot(max(abs(key_checks$total - 1)) < 1e-12)
```

## What changed between the epochs?

These are the fitted **age priors**. The later epoch has a shallower decline,
placing more prior probability on older ages. This changes the reverse
age-length key even though the forward length-at-age model is unchanged.

```{r fitted-age-priors}
bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(calibration_fits)), function(i) {
  delfi_s_age_prior(calibration_fits$log_decline[i], age_grid) |>
    mutate(epoch = calibration_fits$epoch[i])
})) |>
  ggplot(aes(age, p_age, color = epoch)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = epoch_colors, limits = epoch_levels) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Prior probability", color = "Sampling epoch")
```

Now fix a length bin. Each vertical column below is an age distribution and
sums to one. Compare this with the forward-probability heat map above.

```{r posterior-age-heatmaps, fig.height=5.5}
age_key |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = pmax(lower, length_limits[1]), xmax = pmin(upper, length_limits[2]),
                ymin = age - .5, ymax = age + .5, fill = p_age_given_length)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Lbin_cuts, color = "white", linewidth = .25) +
  facet_wrap(~epoch, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "P(age | bin)") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = length_limits) +
  labs(x = "Length bin", y = "Age",
       caption = "Each length-bin column sums to one within its epoch. Growth parameters are fixed in both epochs.")
```

For selected bins, compare the fitted key with the observed conditional age
frequencies. The two-epoch, one-decline-per-epoch model is an approximation;
we should inspect what it can and cannot reproduce.

```{r age-key-diagnostics, fig.height=5.5}
observed_age_frequencies <- aged_counts |>
  group_by(epoch, bin_id) |>
  mutate(observed_probability = if (sum(n_aged) > 0) n_aged / sum(n_aged) else NA_real_) |>
  ungroup()

age_key |>
  filter(bin_id %in% c(3, 6, 9, 12)) |>
  left_join(select(observed_age_frequencies, epoch, bin_id, age, observed_probability),
            by = c("epoch", "bin_id", "age"), relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  mutate(length_bin = factor(length_bin, levels = length_bins$length_bin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(age, p_age_given_length, color = epoch)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .9) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed_probability), alpha = .5, size = 1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~length_bin, ncol = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = epoch_colors, limits = epoch_levels) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Conditional probability", color = "Sampling epoch",
       caption = "Lines: fitted P(age | bin, epoch). Points: observed age frequencies within that bin and epoch.")
```

## Why is this decline not the survival estimate?

Survival helps shape an age distribution, but recruitment history, population
change, and sampling also matter. Under a simple equilibrium with constant
recruitment and constant annual survival $s$, an exponential age decline would
have $d=-\log s$. Mark does **not** impose that relationship here.

Instead, the two declines calibrate age probabilities first. The later kin
model has its own survival parameter, informed by possible births after a
mother's capture. It takes the fitted age keys as fixed, so uncertainty in
this calibration is not propagated into that demographic fit. The two-stage
approximation is part of the model, not a consequence of using tidy tables.

# Prepare the kin-analysis sample

## Apply the length filter and remove individual ages

We now keep female samples with length at most 1.8, as in Mark's driver. Every
retained individual is a potential mother **and** a potential daughter; its
role is not fixed by an age at sampling. Recorded ages are deliberately absent
from `analysis_samples`.

```{r prepare-analysis-samples}
Luplim <- 1.8
Auplim <- 20L
y0 <- min(year_grid)
analysis_bins <- length_bins |> filter(lower <= Luplim)

analysis_samples <- samples |>
  filter(SEX == "FEMALE", LENGTH <= Luplim, Y >= min(year_grid)) |>
  select(ID, Y, LENGTH, bin_id, length_bin, epoch)  # No recorded age A is passed on.

sample_cells <- analysis_samples |>
  count(bin_id, Y, name = "n_sampled") |>
  complete(bin_id = analysis_bins$bin_id, Y = year_grid, fill = list(n_sampled = 0L)) |>
  arrange(bin_id, Y) |>
  mutate(cell_id = row_number())                 # Canonical order: length bin, then year.

analysis_samples <- analysis_samples |>
  left_join(select(sample_cells, bin_id, Y, cell_id),
            by = c("bin_id", "Y"), relationship = "many-to-one")
stopifnot(!"A" %in% names(analysis_samples), !anyNA(analysis_samples$cell_id))

tibble(retained_females = nrow(analysis_samples),
       occupied_length_year_cells = sum(sample_cells$n_sampled > 0),
       years = length(year_grid)) |> knitr::kable()
```

The uppermost retained bin begins at 1.8; it is empty unless an observed length
is exactly that endpoint. Keeping it makes Mark's indexing convention explicit.
Its original calibration probabilities are not merged into the preceding bin.
The inclusion rule for observed samples is still `LENGTH <= 1.8`.

## Build the working age key, including the age-cap approximation

Mark reduces the working age support to 1--20 to speed the kin calculation.
He **lumps all probability at ages 20--40 into the age-20 cell**. This is not
truncation followed by renormalization. The last cell means **20+**, although
subsequent birth-year and survival calculations treat it numerically as age 20.
We retain that approximation and make its tail mass visible.

```{r working-age-key}
age_tail_audit <- age_key |>
  filter(bin_id %in% analysis_bins$bin_id) |>
  summarise(probability_age_20_plus = sum(p_age_given_length[age >= Auplim]),
            .by = c(epoch, bin_id, length_bin))
age_tail_audit |> knitr::kable(digits = 6)

working_age_key <- age_key |>
  filter(bin_id %in% analysis_bins$bin_id) |>
  mutate(age = pmin(age, Auplim)) |>                # Combine older ages in the final cell.
  summarise(p_age_given_length = sum(p_age_given_length), .by = c(epoch, bin_id, age))

age_key_by_year <- expand_grid(year = year_grid, bin_id = analysis_bins$bin_id,
                              age = seq_len(Auplim)) |>
  mutate(epoch = if_else(year <= 2015, epoch_levels[1], epoch_levels[2])) |>
  left_join(working_age_key, by = c("epoch", "bin_id", "age"), relationship = "many-to-one")

working_key_checks <- age_key_by_year |>
  summarise(total = sum(p_age_given_length), .by = c(year, bin_id))
stopifnot(!anyNA(age_key_by_year), max(abs(working_key_checks$total - 1)) < 1e-12)

age_key_by_year |>
  filter(year %in% c(2015, 2016), bin_id == 6) |>
  mutate(age_label = if_else(age == Auplim, paste0(Auplim, "+"), as.character(age))) |>
  select(year, epoch, length_bin = bin_id, age_label, p_age_given_length) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 6)
```

`age_key_by_year` is the explicit lookup table that will connect the covariates
of each comparison to its possible ages. It contains probabilities, not a
point estimate of age for each dolphin.

# Compile the tidy comparison categories

## Count each unordered comparison once

A category is a pair of observed length/year cells. If the cells differ, there
are $n_1n_2$ comparisons. Within one cell of size $n$, there are
$\binom{n}{2}=n(n-1)/2$ comparisons between distinct individuals. We retain only
`cell_1 <= cell_2` to avoid counting both orientations.

Mark instead uses $n^2/2$ for same-cell exposure, a large-sample approximation.
We keep **both columns**, naming the exact one `n_comp` and the Mark-compatible
one `n_comp_mark`. This is bookkeeping about comparisons; it does not remove
either possible biological direction of a POP.

```{r count-comparisons}
comparison_grid <- expand_grid(cell_1 = sample_cells$cell_id, cell_2 = sample_cells$cell_id) |>
  filter(cell_1 <= cell_2) |>
  left_join(transmute(sample_cells, cell_1 = cell_id, L1 = bin_id, Y1 = Y, n1 = n_sampled),
            by = "cell_1", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  left_join(transmute(sample_cells, cell_2 = cell_id, L2 = bin_id, Y2 = Y, n2 = n_sampled),
            by = "cell_2", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  mutate(same_cell = cell_1 == cell_2,
         n_comp = if_else(same_cell, as.double(n1) * (n1 - 1) / 2, as.double(n1) * n2),
         n_comp_mark = if_else(same_cell, as.double(n1)^2 / 2, as.double(n1) * n2))

stopifnot(sum(comparison_grid$n_comp) == choose(nrow(analysis_samples), 2),
          sum(comparison_grid$n_comp_mark) == nrow(analysis_samples)^2 / 2)

comparison_grid |>
  summarise(exact_comparisons = sum(n_comp), Mark_approximation = sum(n_comp_mark),
            difference = sum(n_comp_mark - n_comp)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The approximation adds half the number of sampled individuals to the total
exposure. We will not silently substitute one convention for the other in a
later likelihood comparison.

## Assign identified pairs to the same categories

Both pair endpoints must survive the sample filter. We look up their observed
cells using IDs, then sort the two cell numbers. The original mother/daughter
order and recorded ages play no role in this categorization.

```{r count-observed-pairs}
analysis_pairs <- pairs |>
  inner_join(select(analysis_samples, id_1 = ID, cell_a = cell_id),
             by = "id_1", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  inner_join(select(analysis_samples, id_2 = ID, cell_b = cell_id),
             by = "id_2", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  mutate(cell_1 = pmin(cell_a, cell_b), cell_2 = pmax(cell_a, cell_b))

match_counts <- analysis_pairs |>
  count(cell_1, cell_2, name = "n_MOP")
stopifnot(nrow(anti_join(match_counts, filter(comparison_grid, n_comp > 0),
                        by = c("cell_1", "cell_2"))) == 0)

# Keep zero-match categories; drop only categories with no comparisons.
categories <- comparison_grid |>
  filter(n_comp > 0) |>
  left_join(match_counts, by = c("cell_1", "cell_2"), relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  replace_na(list(n_MOP = 0L)) |>
  left_join(select(length_bins, L1 = bin_id, length_bin_1 = length_bin),
            by = "L1", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  left_join(select(length_bins, L2 = bin_id, length_bin_2 = length_bin),
            by = "L2", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  mutate(epoch_1 = if_else(Y1 <= 2015, epoch_levels[1], epoch_levels[2]),
         epoch_2 = if_else(Y2 <= 2015, epoch_levels[1], epoch_levels[2])) |>
  arrange(cell_1, cell_2)

stopifnot(sum(categories$n_MOP) == nrow(analysis_pairs),
          all(categories$n_MOP <= categories$n_comp), !anyNA(categories))

categories |>
  summarise(categories = n(), comparisons = sum(n_comp), observed_MOPs = sum(n_MOP),
            zero_match_categories = sum(n_MOP == 0)) |> knitr::kable()

categories |>
  select(length_bin_1, Y1, epoch_1, length_bin_2, Y2, epoch_2, n1, n2, n_comp, n_comp_mark, n_MOP) |>
  slice_head(n = 12) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Observed-covariate category table; L1 and L2 in the code are integer bin IDs")
```

A year-by-year summary makes the coverage of the comparison design visible.
The canonical order is by length bin and then year, so cell 1 need not have
been sampled before cell 2. The figure keeps that order; it is not a temporal
parent/offspring assignment.

```{r comparison-heatmap, fig.height=5.5}
categories |>
  summarise(comparisons = sum(n_comp), matches = sum(n_MOP), .by = c(Y1, Y2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Y1, Y2, fill = comparisons / 1000)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = matches), size = 2.7) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#edf3f8", high = "#3C6EA8") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = year_grid) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = year_grid) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = .5)) +
  labs(x = "Sampling year of cell 1", y = "Sampling year of cell 2", fill = "Comparisons\n(thousands)",
       caption = "Fill: exact comparison counts, summed over length bins. Numbers: observed MOPs.")
```

# Work through one category's uncertain ages

The demographic model will have three parameters: log abundance at $y_0$,
exponential growth rate, and annual survival. Here we choose **illustrative
values**, not fitted estimates. We pick one observed off-diagonal category for
inspection; the full category table still retains all zero-match rows.

```{r choose-example-category}
example_category <- categories |>
  filter(n_MOP > 0, !same_cell) |>
  mutate(illustration_priority = Y2 - Y1 >= 6 & Y2 - Y1 <= 10) |>
  arrange(desc(illustration_priority), desc(n_MOP), L1, Y1, L2, Y2) |>
  slice_head(n = 1) |>
  select(-illustration_priority)
example_parameters <- list(log_N0 = log(5000), growth_rate = 0.01,
                           annual_survival = 0.8, y0 = y0, maturity_age = Amat)
example_category |>
  select(length_bin_1, Y1, length_bin_2, Y2, n_comp, n_MOP) |>
  knitr::kable()
tibble(parameter = names(example_parameters), value = unlist(example_parameters)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

For possible ages $a_1,a_2$, birth years are $b_1=y_1-a_1$ and $b_2=y_2-a_2$.
If individual 2 is the mother of individual 1, the conditional probability is

\[
q_{2\to1}(a_1,a_2)=
\mathbf{1}\{b_1\ge b_2+A_{\mathrm{mat}}\}
\frac{s^{\max(0,b_1-y_2)}}{N_{b_1}}.
\]

The indicator requires maturity at the daughter's birth. If that birth is
no later than the mother's capture, we already know she survived to it. If
it is later, survival from capture to birth contributes the power of $s$.
The reverse direction exchanges 1 and 2. At any fixed pair of true ages,
both directions cannot hold simultaneously.

Let $w_i(a_i)=P(A_i=a_i\mid L_i,y_i)$ be the conditional age weights for
individual $i$, distinct from the marginal age prior $\pi_e(a)$. The mixed
probability is

\[
p_c=\sum_{a_1=1}^{20}\sum_{a_2=1}^{20}
w_1(a_1)w_2(a_2)
\{q_{2\to1}(a_1,a_2)+q_{1\to2}(a_1,a_2)\}.
\]

The helper expands those **400 terms** into a tibble. Open its definition in
`R/tidy-delfi-S.R`: both directions and their survival exponents are explicit.

Here is how the equation maps to its columns. Sampling years are fixed by the
chosen category; ages and implied birth years vary across the 400 rows.

| Column | Term in the equation |
|:--|:--|
| `age_1`, `age_2` | $a_1,a_2$, the possible ages at capture |
| `sampling_year_1`, `sampling_year_2` | $y_1,y_2$, the observed capture years |
| `birth_1`, `birth_2` | $b_1=y_1-a_1$, $b_2=y_2-a_2$ |
| `p_age_1`, `p_age_2` | $w_1(a_1),w_2(a_2)$ |
| `joint_age_probability` | $w_1(a_1)w_2(a_2)$ |
| `mature_2_at_birth_1` | $\mathbf{1}\{b_1\ge b_2+A_{\mathrm{mat}}\}$ |
| `future_years_2_to_1` | $\max(0,b_1-y_2)$ |
| `N_at_birth_1` | $N_{b_1}$ |
| `p_2_mother_of_1` | $q_{2\to1}(a_1,a_2)$ |
| `contribution_2_to_1` | $w_1(a_1)w_2(a_2)q_{2\to1}(a_1,a_2)$ |
| `contribution` | $w_1(a_1)w_2(a_2)\{q_{2\to1}+q_{1\to2}\}$, one complete summand |

In particular, `future_years_2_to_1` counts the years **after individual 2's
capture until individual 1's birth**, or zero if that birth preceded capture.
Remember that $y_2=b_2+a_2$. The reverse-direction columns exchange 1 and 2;
thus `future_years_1_to_2` is $\max(0,b_2-y_1)$, with $y_1=b_1+a_1$.

Thus `contribution_2_to_1` is the entire weighted term for individual 2 being
the mother, not just its survival factor:

\[
w_1(a_1)w_2(a_2)q_{2\to1}(a_1,a_2)
=w_1(a_1)w_2(a_2)
\mathbf{1}\{b_1\ge b_2+A_{\mathrm{mat}}\}
\frac{s^{\max(0,b_1-y_2)}}{N_{b_1}}.
\]

The table below displays selected columns; the full tibble also contains the
individual age weights, maturity indicators, abundances, and conditional
probabilities listed above.

```{r expand-example-ages}
age_pairs <- do.call(delfi_s_age_pair_example,
  c(list(category = example_category, age_key_by_year = age_key_by_year), example_parameters))
example_probability <- sum(age_pairs$contribution)
stopifnot(nrow(age_pairs) == Auplim^2,
          abs(sum(age_pairs$joint_age_probability) - 1) < 1e-12,
          !any(age_pairs$mature_2_at_birth_1 & age_pairs$mature_1_at_birth_2),
          is.finite(example_probability), example_probability > 0)

age_pairs |>
  arrange(desc(contribution)) |>
  select(age_1, age_2, sampling_year_1, sampling_year_2, birth_1, birth_2, joint_age_probability,
         future_years_2_to_1, future_years_1_to_2,
         contribution_2_to_1, contribution_1_to_2) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 8, caption = "The ten largest age-pair contributions at the illustrative parameters")
```

```{r one-age-row, include=FALSE}
worked_age_row <- age_pairs |>
  slice_max(contribution_1_to_2, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
```

To read one row numerically, consider the largest `contribution_1_to_2`.
Individual 1 was sampled in `r worked_age_row$sampling_year_1`; at possible
age `r worked_age_row$age_1`, its birth year is `r worked_age_row$birth_1`.
Individual 2 was sampled in `r worked_age_row$sampling_year_2`; at possible
age `r worked_age_row$age_2`, its birth year is `r worked_age_row$birth_2`.
For individual 1 to be the mother, she must survive from her capture in
`r worked_age_row$sampling_year_1` until the daughter's birth in
`r worked_age_row$birth_2`. Thus `future_years_1_to_2` is
$\max(0,\,`r worked_age_row$birth_2`-`r worked_age_row$sampling_year_1`)=`r worked_age_row$future_years_1_to_2`$,
and the survival factor is
$`r example_parameters$annual_survival`^{`r worked_age_row$future_years_1_to_2`}$.
Multiplying this by the maturity indicator, dividing by `N_at_birth_2`, and
multiplying by `joint_age_probability` gives `contribution_1_to_2`.
Summing both directional contributions over all rows gives $p_c$.

In the next figure, the first panel is the age-mixture weight alone. The other
panels show each direction's contribution to the total POP probability.
Impossible age combinations have zero contribution. Filled circles mark the
largest contributing age pair in each relationship direction. Dashed boundaries
separate combinations requiring survival beyond capture from those that do not.

```{r age-pair-heatmaps, fig.height=4}
age_pair_plot_data <- age_pairs |>
  transmute(age_1, age_2,
    `Age-mixture weight` = joint_age_probability,
    `Individual 2 is mother of 1` = contribution_2_to_1 / example_probability,
    `Individual 1 is mother of 2` = contribution_1_to_2 / example_probability) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(age_1, age_2), names_to = "panel", values_to = "probability") |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = c("Age-mixture weight",
    "Individual 2 is mother of 1", "Individual 1 is mother of 2")))

largest_contributions <- age_pair_plot_data |>
  filter(panel != "Age-mixture weight") |>
  slice_max(probability, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE, by = panel) |>
  filter(probability > 0)

survival_boundaries <- tibble(
  panel = factor(c("Individual 2 is mother of 1", "Individual 1 is mother of 2"),
    levels = levels(age_pair_plot_data$panel)),
  boundary = c(example_category$Y1 - example_category$Y2,
               example_category$Y2 - example_category$Y1) - 0.5
)

panel_labels <- c(
  "Age-mixture weight" = "Age-mixture weight\n(all possible ages)",
  "Individual 2 is mother of 1" = paste0("Individual 2 is mother of 1\n",
    sprintf("%.1f%% of the POP probability", 100 * sum(age_pairs$contribution_2_to_1) / example_probability)),
  "Individual 1 is mother of 2" = paste0("Individual 1 is mother of 2\n",
    sprintf("%.1f%% of the POP probability", 100 * sum(age_pairs$contribution_1_to_2) / example_probability))
)

age_pair_plot_data |>
  ggplot(aes(age_1, age_2, fill = probability)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_vline(data = filter(survival_boundaries, panel == "Individual 2 is mother of 1", boundary > 0),
             aes(xintercept = boundary), inherit.aes = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", color = "white") +
  geom_hline(data = filter(survival_boundaries, panel == "Individual 1 is mother of 2", boundary > 0),
             aes(yintercept = boundary), inherit.aes = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", color = "white") +
  geom_point(data = largest_contributions, aes(age_1, age_2), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 21, fill = "white", color = "black", size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1, labeller = as_labeller(panel_labels)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Probability\nweight", transform = "sqrt") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 15, 20), labels = c("1", "5", "10", "15", "20+")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 15, 20), labels = c("1", "5", "10", "15", "20+")) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Possible age of individual 1 at capture", y = "Possible age of individual 2 at capture",
       caption = paste("Age-mixture panel sums to 1; the two contribution panels sum to 1 jointly.",
         "Square-root color scale makes small contributions more visible.", sep = "\n"))
```

The same calculation supplies this row's expected match count. This is one
row's Poisson contribution at the example parameters, **not a fitted model**.

```{r example-row-result}
example_result <- example_category |>
  transmute(length_bin_1, Y1, length_bin_2, Y2, n_comp, n_MOP,
            p_MOP = example_probability,
            expected_MOP = n_comp * p_MOP,
            loglik_piece = dpois(n_MOP, expected_MOP, log = TRUE))
example_result |> knitr::kable(digits = 8)

age_pairs |>
  summarise(probability_2_mother_of_1 = sum(contribution_2_to_1),
            probability_1_mother_of_2 = sum(contribution_1_to_2),
            fraction_requiring_postcapture_survival =
              (sum(contribution_2_to_1[future_years_2_to_1 > 0]) +
               sum(contribution_1_to_2[future_years_1_to_2 > 0])) / example_probability) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 8)
```

# What is ready for the likelihood?

We now have two explicit inputs:

* `categories`: observed length/year categories, comparison exposure, and MOP
  counts, including the zero-match categories.
* `age_key_by_year`: the calibrated probability distribution over working ages
  for each observed length/year cell.

The demographic parameters will change the abundance and survival factors.
The age-mixture probabilities and maturity conditions can be prepared in advance.
The next stage will turn the one-row reference calculation into an efficient
full objective and compare it with Mark's implementation.

<details class="optional-checks">
<summary>Optional checks: compare calibration and category counts with Mark's functions</summary>

These checks use the chosen dataset's `r-scripts/ckmr_funs.r`; they do not run
the interactive driver. Set `check_mark_code: false` to skip execution. The tidy
preparation above does not require Mark's packages.

```{r compare-with-mark, message=FALSE}
mark_repo <- dirname(dirname(data_path))
mark_functions <- file.path(mark_repo, "r-scripts", "ckmr_funs.r")
mark_packages <- c("mvbutils", "offarray", "atease", "kinsimmer2")
can_check <- isTRUE(params$check_mark_code) && file.exists(mark_functions) &&
  all(vapply(mark_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE))

if (can_check) {
  library(mvbutils)
  library(offarray)
  library(atease)
  library(kinsimmer2)
  mark_code <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
  sys.source(mark_functions, envir = mark_code)
  mark_labels <- levels(mvbutils::mcut(2, Lbin_cuts))
  mark_forward <- offarray(0, dimseq = list(Lb = mark_labels, A = age_grid))
  mark_forward[] <- length_probs |>
    arrange(age, bin_id) |>
    pull(p_length_given_age)
  mark_key_by_year <- offarray(0, dimseq = list(A = age_grid, Lb = mark_labels, Y = year_grid))

  calibration_comparison <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(calibration_fits)), function(i) {
    e <- calibration_fits$epoch[i]
    n <- filter(aged_counts, epoch == e) |> arrange(bin_id, age) |> pull(n_aged)
    counts <- offarray(0, dimseq = list(A = age_grid, Lb = mark_labels))
    counts[] <- n
    mark_env <- list2env(list(Pr_Lb_A = mark_forward, nA_Lb = counts,
      AGES = age_grid, Lbins = mark_labels, Pr_A = -1, Pr_A_Lb = -1), parent = mark_code)
    mark_alk <- mark_code$ALK_delfi_S
    environment(mark_alk) <- mark_env
    mark_ll <- mark_alk(calibration_fits$log_decline[i])
    tidy_key <- age_key |>
      filter(epoch == e) |> arrange(bin_id, age) |> pull(p_age_given_length)
    tibble(epoch = e,
      loglik_difference = mark_ll - calibration_fits$conditional_log_likelihood[i],
      max_age_probability_difference = max(abs(as.numeric(mark_env$Pr_A_Lb) - tidy_key)))
  }))
  stopifnot(max(abs(calibration_comparison$loglik_difference)) < 1e-7,
            max(calibration_comparison$max_age_probability_difference) < 1e-10)
  knitr::kable(calibration_comparison, digits = 10)

  # Populate this adapter explicitly, outside the per-epoch checking function.
  # Each matrix has age in rows and length bin in columns.
  for (year in year_grid) {
    e <- if (year <= 2015) epoch_levels[1] else epoch_levels[2]
    probabilities <- age_key |> filter(epoch == e) |>
      arrange(bin_id, age) |> pull(p_age_given_length)
    mark_key_by_year[, , year] <- matrix(probabilities, nrow = length(age_grid))
  }

  mark_prepared <- mark_code$boring_data_prep_delfi_S(raw_data,
    Pr_A_LY = mark_key_by_year, Lbin_cuts = Lbin_cuts, Luplim = Luplim, Auplim = Auplim,
    prev_env = mark_code)
  mark_categories <- mark_code$boring_dfize(mark_prepared$n_MOP_LY1LY2,
                                          mark_prepared$n_comp_MOP_LY1LY2) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    transmute(L1 = match(as.character(L1), mark_prepared$Lbins), Y1,
              L2 = match(as.character(L2), mark_prepared$Lbins), Y2,
              n_comp_mark = n_comp_MOP, n_MOP) |>
    arrange(L1, Y1, L2, Y2)
  tidy_mark_categories <- comparison_grid |>
    filter(n_comp_mark > 0) |>
    left_join(match_counts, by = c("cell_1", "cell_2"), relationship = "one-to-one") |>
    replace_na(list(n_MOP = 0L)) |>
    select(L1, Y1, L2, Y2, n_comp_mark, n_MOP) |>
    arrange(L1, Y1, L2, Y2)
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.data.frame(mark_categories), as.data.frame(tidy_mark_categories),
                            check.attributes = FALSE)))
  tibble(check = c("Calibration likelihoods and age probabilities", "Mark-compatible category counts"),
         result = "Agree") |> knitr::kable()

  # Check all 400 worked-example terms against Mark's directed age mixture.
  mark_loglik <- mark_code$generic_lglk_MOP_livel_mammal
  mark_prepared$B_range <- seq.int(min(year_grid) - Auplim, max(year_grid) - 1)
  environment(mark_loglik) <- mark_prepared
  mark_loglik(c(example_parameters$log_N0, example_parameters$growth_rate,
                qlogis(example_parameters$annual_survival)))
  row <- example_category
  mark_probability <- mark_prepared$Pr_MOP_LY1LY2[
    mark_prepared$Lbins[row$L1], row$Y1, mark_prepared$Lbins[row$L2], row$Y2]
  stopifnot(abs(as.numeric(mark_probability) - example_probability) < 1e-12)
  tibble(tidy_example_probability = example_probability,
         Mark_example_probability = as.numeric(mark_probability)) |>
    knitr::kable(digits = 10)
} else {
  cat("Mark-code checks skipped. They require check_mark_code = TRUE, the function file,\n",
      "and packages: ", paste(mark_packages, collapse = ", "), ".\n", sep = "")
}
```

There is an additional same-cell convention to resolve before fitting the full
model: Mark halves the sum of the two directed probabilities when both members
have the same observed length/year category. Same-cell exposure already has a
half-factor. For exact unordered pairs of distinct individuals, the two possible
mother/daughter directions are mutually exclusive and their probabilities add.
Our worked example deliberately uses different cells, where this issue does
not arise and both calculations agree. The exact and Mark-compatible exposure
columns above keep the bookkeeping differences visible for the next stage.

</details>

```{r session-information}
sessionInfo()
```
